%c[ui_gray_1]A homemade portable hand-cranked generator built around a single-phase asynchronous motor salvaged from an old appliance. Its output passes through a step-down transformer to a rectifier made with Soviet D242 diodes, which charges a Portable Power Unit. A capacitor connected to the motor’s auxiliary winding provides self-excitation. The rotor is turned through a worm drive at its rated speed of 1,300–1,500 rpm. It has an American WESTON ELECTRICAL INSTRUMENT needle ammeter. The device is heavy, but highly valued in the Zone; skilled craftsmen can improve it.

An American hand-held fragmentation grenade. The M67 uses an M213 fuse with two safety devices: a standard ring-pull pin and a wire loop wrapped around the fuse to hold the lever. Its reliable safety allows it to be carried by hooking the fuse lever to a gear belt. Its compact size and dense fragmentation made the M67 popular with paratroopers, marines and special forces.

\n \n%c[ui_gray_1]A large multipurpose knife with a dependable rubberized grip, often used by US soldiers since 1986. It is sharp and in good condition. Although ineffective against body armor, its serrated blade cuts flesh well and keeps wounds from closing. This makes it ideal for finishing wounded animals or silently attacking sentries.

\n \n%c[ui_gray_1]A modern, very sturdy stainless-steel hunting knife. Its finely finished blade cuts the hides and soft tissue of even large mutants with ease. It is also excellent for hunting, as it can inflict deep, bleeding wounds. However, the blade is not designed to pierce body armor, which greatly limits its use.

%c[ui_gray_1]This Soviet steel knife has a 152 mm blade with a large finger choil, a black wooden handle and an S-shaped guard. The reverse guard reflects the standard Soviet grip, with the blade facing inward. A rough fabric wrap reinforces the handle for a better grip. The knife is fairly small and cannot inflict deep wounds, but it can pierce body armor.

\n \n%c[ui_gray_1]NOT USED! A very rare Soviet military knife of historic and symbolic significance. Its wooden handle bears a metal Airborne Forces emblem from the Great Patriotic War. Such knives are awarded to stalkers for exceptional service, for example for rescuing a faction leader during a mission. Any stalker carrying one is sure to be respected in the Zone.

A folding knife of exceptional quality, ideal for a scout. It is a lethal weapon and the only knife in the Zone that can both pierce body armor and inflict serious wounds on unprotected flesh. An excellent close-combat weapon.

The compact 9A-91 carbine was developed in 1992 by the Tula Instrument Design Bureau as a more advanced rival to the SR-3 Vikhr. Its gas-operated action locks by rotating a bolt with four lugs. The hammer-fired trigger supports both semi-automatic and fully automatic fire. The safety and fire selector sits above the trigger guard on the left; on the modernized version it is on the right to make room for an optics rail. Early models had a muzzle brake, later removed. The stock folds upward and forward. Apart from the plastic pistol grip and handguard, the weapon is steel. It can be concealed easily, and its charging handle folds for carry. Unlike an AK, the charging-handle slot remains open.

The 1994 Nikonov AN-94 “Abakan” is based on the Kalashnikov system. Its key combat feature is a two-round burst mode with a high rate of fire. Recoil begins to affect the shooter only after both bullets have left the barrel, improving accuracy and shot grouping. Special forces operatives and Duty fighters use it to engage enemies wearing body armor at relatively long range.

The Galil ACE family of assault rifles is developed and manufactured by Israel Weapon Industries (IWI). Its design is based on the Galil, itself derived from the Kalashnikov AK. The ACE line emphasizes ergonomics, ease of use, accessory compatibility and flexibility. It covers three of the world’s most common cartridges—5.56×45 NATO, 7.62×39 M43 and 7.62×51 NATO—with several barrel lengths. Compared with earlier models, the charging handle was moved to the left so the shooter can cycle it without releasing the firing grip. The rifle also gained a bolt catch, integral Picatinny rails for optics and accessories, and an adjustable telescoping stock.

The AK-12 is a 2012 Kalashnikov assault rifle design. Its controls were extensively revised for easier use: the safety/fire selector was changed and duplicated on the left side, and a bolt catch was added with controls on both sides. Another new feature is the use of Picatinny rails. Compared with the 5.45×39 mm AK-74M and 7.62×39 mm AKM, the AK-12 offers improved ergonomics. The development work improved accuracy and mechanism reliability and extended service life. It uses a long-stroke gas piston and rotating bolt; its bolt group and trigger mechanism were substantially revised from the AK-74. The rifle has a new adjustable polymer telescoping stock that folds to either side, with adjustable length and cheek height. The bore axis is aligned with the stock, as on AR-15 assault rifles, reducing the recoil moment and improving accuracy.

In the mid-1980s, designers at the Izhevsk Machine-Building Plant developed several universal modified Kalashnikov rifle prototypes, the A-60 and A-61. The AK-74M, a successful 5.45×39 mm model, was developed from them. Its design largely repeats the AK-74 and has no fundamental internal differences. It retains the best qualities of Kalashnikov rifles while adding features that improve combat and service performance. The AK-74M embodies the idea of a universal rifle, replacing four models at once: the AK-74, AK-74N, AKS-74 and AKS-74N.

The APB (Avtomaticheskiy Pistolet Beshumnyy, silent automatic pistol) is a suppressed version of the APS. It passed trials and entered service in 1972, first with Soviet special forces and later with special units in former Soviet countries. It saw extensive use during the conflict in Afghanistan and in local conflicts across the former USSR. With its stock and suppressor attached, it was often carried on a shoulder strap and used as a primary weapon. It differs little from the standard APS.\n \n

The large-caliber 12.7 mm ASH-12 assault rifle was developed at TsKIB SOO for Russian FSB special-purpose units, alongside the VSSK sniper rifle.
